question: Did Athens have a genuine case against Socrates, beyond religious prejudice?
answer: His circle had nearly wrecked the city. Alcibiades, his favourite, defected to Sparta; Critias, another associate, led the Thirty Tyrants, who put more than a thousand citizens to death. Socrates mocked choosing officials by lot. An amnesty in 403 BC barred prosecution for political acts, so impiety and corrupting the young were the charges left.
move: It turns on whether the company someone kept can ever be enough to convict.
ask: Do I judge people by what they did or by the company they kept?
counterpoint: Socrates refused the Thirty's order to arrest Leon of Salamis for execution, and in 406 BC he alone of the presiding councillors opposed an illegal mass trial of generals under the democracy. He wrote nothing and led no faction. Condemning a man for his friends and his questions is what Athenian free speech was meant to prevent.
reference: Stone, The Trial of Socrates, Little, Brown, 1988
